lesson_title: The Choir at the Door: Labour Rights and Collective Bargaining
hook_text: One packer complains, nothing happens. Every packer complains — everything changes.
clip_script: Imagine Thabo, a packer at a distribution warehouse, knocking on the supervisor's door: the pay is too little, the night shifts too long. Through the window, the supervisor can see the morning queue at the fence — dozens of people hoping for exactly his job. How hard does one complaint land? It barely lands at all. One worker alone is a voice shouting against the wind. Now replay the scene with every packer standing at that door, one person speaking for all of them: the pay is too little — for every one of us. The calculation has changed completely. The supervisor is no longer comparing one replaceable worker with a queue; he is comparing an entire warehouse falling silent with the orders that must ship tonight. That is a union in a single scene — and the Constitution doesn't just allow it, it guarantees it: join, organise, bargain, and when every road closes, strike. Behind that door stand three rulebooks — one for the argument day, one floor under every ordinary day, one fund for the worst day — and when talks jam, a free referee's room with a three-rung ladder: talk, proposals, decision. The factory's oldest quarrel, rewritten as rules.
visual_style: A single small figure at a huge door with wind lines streaming past, then dozens of figures merging into one large chorus silhouette; three glowing rulebooks sliding onto a shelf; a ladder rising rung by rung inside a whistle-marked room.
pacing: Slow lone-knock open, surge at the gathered door, brisk tour of rulebooks and ladder, firm close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and walk into your first job knowing the rules.
